newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: PORT HEDLAND DISPUTE AFFECTING WA'S FUTURE, SAYS CHAMBER
The Western Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry says unions involved in an industrial stand-off at a project at Port Hedland, are playing with the state's future.

More than six-hundred workers on the A$1 billion construction of BHP's hot-briquette iron processing plant, voted yesterday to reject a four per cent pay increase, defying an Industrial Relations Commission recommendation to return to work.
The workers want wages up to 38 per cent above award rates, and a living away from home allowance of 500 dollars-a-week.
The Chamber of Commerce and Industry's Chris Mitsopoulos says the workers haven't been paid since New Year, and the contractors are losing money as well.
Mr Mitsopoulos says the action isn't only affecting the Port Hedland project.
He says there are other parties considering similar projects in the state, who may be swayed by the dispute.
WIFE OF MURDERED JOURNALIST SAYS CONSPIRACY SHOCKING
The British Government has released details of the burial of five Australians murdered in East Timor during an invasion in 1975.
Shirley Shackleton, whose journalist husband Greg was among those murdered, says governments in Australia and Britain conspired to keep burial details from the victims' families.
She says she always felt the truth would always come out, but describes the conspiracy all these years as shocking.
US DID THE RIGHT THING WITH MEXICO LOAN, SAYS CLINTON
Bill Clinton says Americans can feel proud they did the right thing, after announcing Mexico would repay a multi-billion dollar loan in full three years ahead of schedule.
The President says Mexico will pay the final US$4.8 billion dollar installment of an eighteen billion dollar loan, taken out two years ago following the Peso's collapse.
The bailout was criticised by some republicans in Congress, but President Clinton says the transaction earned the U-S more than half a billion dollars.
KOALAS DECISION EXPECTED BY TOMORROW
In New South Wales, a decision is expected by tomorrow on an application by the Hunter Koala Preservation Society, which wants 60 koalas killed.
The society wants to kill the koalas, saying they'll infect other colonies if they're moved away from a sandmining operation near Newcastle.
It's the first time a conservation group has applied to the Service for a licence to kill koalas.
The Society says it wants to ensure the koalas have a humane death rather than being dislocated by the sandmining.
But the National Parks and Wildlife Service says the Society's application will be rejected unless it can provide more evidence in support.
NOT ENOUGH TIME FOR ADELAIDE SAILOR
The captain of the HMAS Adelaide which rescued yachtsman Tony Bullimore says it's likely there'll be no time for the proposed party for the 144 sailors involved in the operation.
During the euphoria of his rescue from the Southern Ocean, Mr Bullimore said he'd host a party for his rescuers.

Captain Raydon Gates says the Briton wouldn't be held to his promise. Navy public relations officer, Vic Jeffery, says most of the sailors went back on leave when the ship returned on Monday, and they'll be settinG sail early next week to meet Australia Day commitments in Hobart.
FOUR IRAQIS WASHED UP IN AUSTRALIA BLAME SADDAM
Four men found wandering on a Torres Strait island yesterday morning, have told local authorities they fled Iraq because Saddam Hussein was killing people.
The illegal immigrants were found by community police officers on Saibai Island, walking through a village.
Island Chairman and the Acting head the Torres Strait Regional Authority, Terry Waia WIRE says one of the men he questioned said they left Iraq on a boat heading towards Darwin.
Mr Waia says it's the first time Iraqi Nationals had arrived in the Torres Strait as illegal immigrants.
JOCKEY PAY CLAIM NEGOTIATIONS CONTINUING TODAY
Negotiations will continue today in a bid to resolve the industrial dispute between the nation's jockeys, the Australian Jockey Club and Principal Racing clubs over riding fees.
Jockeys, supported in their new affiliation with the Australian Workers' Union, want a 60-dollar increase in the losing riding fee to A$135.
They've been offered a A$15 a ride increase, but say that's not good enough when many of them are living below the poverty line.
AWU Assistant National Secretary, Chris Hayes says he'll be asking mediator, New South Wales Racing Minister Richard Face, to improve the offer.
Earlier this month jockeys took strike action over the dispute.
CLAIMS GOVERNOR'S MOVE COSTS MORE
The New South Wales Opposition says its calculations show moving the NSW Governor out of Government House has cost the taxpayer more money, than if he'd stayed on.
Twelve months ago the Carr government brought an end to the official status of Government House as the Governor's residence, when it appointed Gordon Samuels.

Opposition leader, Peter Collins, says additional security, renting another office, redundancies and extra staff means the new arrangement costs a million dollars more than if the Governor lived and worked at Government House.
He says it's an embarassing and costly failure for the State government, and that Premier Bob Carr should apologise.
ELLE RACING YACHT SKIPPER TO APPEAR IN COURT
The dispute involving the former skipper of the all-female racing yacht "Elle Racing", will be back in the Federal Court in Sydney this morning.
The management group for the yacht says attempts yesterday to reach an out of court settlement with former skipper Adrienne Cahalan were unsuccessful.
Ms Cahalan is suing the yacht-racing syndicate for A$97,000 in alleged unpaid wages.
As part of the legal manoeuvrings, lawyers for Ms Cahalan have successfully applied to have the 18-metre "Elle Racing" impounded in Sydney's Darling Harbour.
